bio.en: Sarah Tavel is a partner at Benchmark, one of the world's preeminent venture capital firms, focusing on consumer and marketplace startups, and was the first product manager at Pinterest.
bio.zh: Sarah Tavel 是 Benchmark 的合伙人，该基金是全球最负盛名的风投机构之一，她专注投资消费级与 marketplace 类初创公司，此前曾是 Pinterest 的首位产品经理。

summary.en: Sarah brings a product-and-growth leader's lens to venture investing, sharing how she evaluates consumer and marketplace startups from first principles. She discusses what makes a compelling founder and product, the metrics and motions that signal durable growth, and lessons from her own operating background at Pinterest. The episode is a rare blend of investor and product-leader thinking applied to building and backing companies.
summary.zh: Sarah 以产品与增长领导者的视角看待风险投资，分享了她如何从源头（first principles）评估消费级与 marketplace 初创公司。她讨论了什么造就一个有吸引力的创始人与产品、哪些指标与打法预示着可持续的增长，以及她在 Pinterest 的运营背景中获得的经验。本期罕见地将投资者与产品领导者的思维融合，应用于打造与押注公司。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: I think a lot of people think about markets almost like these bodies of water, it's like it's this big body of water that we're going after. I actually think that the most interesting markets, you have to think of them like currents where you're there's something happening in the market that's creating this current where you can have a plank of wood that you've put on the river and it's going to pull you forward. Versus a market that doesn't really have that momentum to it, you're going to have to build something really big and fancy to make any progress. That's why we care less about market size because really, what you're looking for when you're looking at a market, are what are the dynamics of change, what's the current and momentum that's going to pull the company and make the job easier for the founders to actually build something that endures.
turns.zh: 我觉得很多人想市场，差不多像这些水体，像是我们去追逐的一大片水域。我其实觉得，最有趣的市场，你得把它们想成洋流——市场里正发生着什么，创造出这股洋流，让你放一块木板在河上，它就会把你往前拉。相比之下，一个没有那种势能的市场，你得建个又大又花哨的东西才能取得任何进展。那正是我们不太在乎市场规模的原因——真的，你看一个市场时寻找的，是变化的动力、是那股会把公司往前拉、让创始人更容易建出能持久的东西的洋流和动量。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Super excited to be here.
turns.zh: 超级兴奋来到这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you may or may not know this, but actually, normally have a policy of no VCs on the podcast. But you're a very special VC because you're a former product manager. Many people don't know you were the first product manager at Pinterest. To me, you still think like a product manager so I'm very excited to break my rule and have you on the podcast.
turns.zh: 所以你可能知道也可能不知道，我通常有个"不请 VC 上播客"的原则。但你是个非常特别的 VC，因为你以前是产品经理。很多人不知道你是 Pinterest 的第一位产品经理。对我来说，你思考方式仍像个产品经理，所以我非常兴奋破例请你上播客。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Thank you for the exception.
turns.zh: 谢谢破例。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I want to do with our time together is dig into two frameworks that you've developed and use with founders that you work with to help them build successful companies. One is focused around customer businesses, and one marketplace businesses. (00:03:49): Let's just start with the first framework. I think you call it the Hierarchy of Engagement. Just to start, could you maybe just share a broad overview of this framework? And also, just where it emerged from, where you came up with this concept?
turns.zh: 我想用我们共处的时间，深挖你开发、并和你合作的创始人一起用的两个框架，帮他们建成功的公司。一个聚焦消费（用户）业务，一个聚焦市场业务。(00:03:49): 就从第一个框架开始。我想你叫它"参与度层级"（Hierarchy of Engagement）。开头能否先给个这个框架的宏观概览？还有，它从哪来、你哪想出这个概念？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Sure. I think one thing you'll notice about me is that I have an allergic reaction to vanity metrics, what people talk about as vanity metrics. When I made the transition from Pinterest, where I was leading product for the discovery team, so I was responsible for all the discovery surfaces on Pinterest. The home feed, the search, the recommendations, a couple other teams. Ultimately, what those teams were about was about engagement, increasing engagement of Pinterest. It was helping people, when they were on Pinterest, find something that they loved enough that they wanted to pin it to one of their boards. (00:04:48): When I started to meet with all these really talented consumer founders building consumer social products, this was during a time when everybody was getting excited about growth hacking. What you would see is that you would see all these founders coming in, and they all had these up and to the right graphs, whether it was sign-ups, or downloads, or MAUs. It felt to me like it wasn't obvious that those metrics that they were all getting very attached, and focused on, and showing in these presentations was the wrong thing to focus on. It didn't get to the heart of whether they were on the path to building enduring consumer social product. They were missing, at the core, the criticality of engagement. (00:05:45): I just started to feel this and it became like a pebble in my shoe. I started just to go through that process that you've gone through many times before of writing and distilling it, and that's where I came up with this hierarchy. What you realize when you look at social products is that they're almost is this action which I call the core action of that product that forms the foundation of the product. When a user completes this action, it's clear that they both understand the utility of the product, they understand what that product is all about, and it's an action that, if they perform the action, they're very likely to come back. So for Facebook, the obvious action is friending, in the beginning days. For Pinterest, it's pinning. I don't know if you're an Evernote user. For Evernote, it's writing a note. When you perform that action, that means you're an engaged user. Of course, there's a lot of other actions that you have to do. You can follow people on Pinterest, you comment on Facebook. But the end of the day, if you're not doing that action, you're not really a user to the product. That's why the MAU thing doesn't really mean anything. It's really looking at, I think, of users completing the core action. You can look at this as a cohort, weekly, daily, whatever the right cadence is. But that's the foundation, that's level one.
turns.zh: 当然。我觉得你会注意到我的一点，是我对虚荣指标（vanity metrics）有过敏反应。当我从 Pinterest 转型时，我领导的是发现（discovery）team 的产品，负责 Pinterest 上所有发现面：首页 feed、搜索、推荐，还有几个团队。说到底，那些团队是关于参与度的，提升 Pinterest 的参与度。它帮人们在 Pinterest 上时，找到足够喜欢、想 pin 到自己某个画板上的东西。(00:04:48): 当我开始见这些很有才华的消费创始人、建消费社交产品时，那正是大家都对增长黑客兴奋的时候。你会看到所有这些创始人进来，都有那些右上扬的图，无论是注册、下载还是 MAU。给我的感觉是，他们全都执着、聚焦、在演示里展示的那些指标，并不明显是错的关注点。它没触及核心：他们是否在通往建一个持久消费社交产品的路上。他们 missing，在核心上，参与度的关键性。(00:05:45): 我就开始有这种感觉，像鞋里的一颗石子。我就开始走你走过很多次的那个过程——写下来、提炼它，那就是我得出这个层级的地方。看社交产品时你会意识到，几乎都有一个动作——我称为那个产品的核心动作（core action）——构成产品的基础。当用户完成这个动作，很清楚他们既理解了产品的效用、理解产品是干嘛的，而且这是个动作——如果他们做了，他们极可能回来。所以 Facebook，早期明显的动作是加好友（friending）。Pinterest 是 pin（钉）。我不知道你是不是 Evernote 用户。Evernote 是写一条笔记。当你做了那个动作，意味着你是个参与的用户。当然还有很多其他动作你得做。你可以在 Pinterest 关注人、在 Facebook 评论。但说到底，如果你不做那个动作，你就不是产品真正的用户。那就是 MAU 那东西其实没意义的原因。真正要看的，我觉得，是用户完成核心动作。你可以按同期群、周、日，看对的节奏。但那是基础，是第一层。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Basically, there's some definition of an active user that a consumer business basically needs to define, and essential figure out what is that action they're taking that makes them an active user versus just opening up the app, or whatever it is. For Snapchat, it might be sending a snap.
turns.zh: 基本上，消费业务基本需要定义一个"活跃用户"是什么，并想清楚那个让他们成为活跃用户、而非只是打开 App 的动作是什么。Snapchat 可能是发一个 snap。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For What's App, it might be sending a message. Okay, cool.
turns.zh: WhatsApp 可能是发一条消息。好，酷。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Yes. Yes. By the way, this action, it's very important to pick the right action. You want to make sure it's an action that scales to enough users. You want to think about, "If I think about my product roadmap and optimize for it, what do we end up doing?" (00:07:56): Just to give you a more concrete example, actually in the early days of Pinterest, we weren't sure what it was. We had all these things we were measuring. We were measuring follows, we were measuring clicking through, liking something, pinning obviously, time on site. We would do these experiments and you would get all this different data where some things would go up, some things would go down. What were we optimizing for? (00:08:24): There's something that's really, really important about having that clarity of this is the action that is most important for our product. All things, our NUX has to lead to this. If a user isn't doing this, then there's something missing from their experience of the product. It's super important to get real clarity and know exactly the one that you're going to be picking to go forward.
turns.zh: 对。对。顺便，这个动作，选对动作非常重要。你要确保它是能扩展到足够多用户的动作。你要想"如果我想产品路线图、为它优化，我们最终会做什么？"(00:07:56): 给你个更具体的例子，其实在 Pinterest 早期，我们不确定它是什么。我们测了一大堆东西。我们测关注、测点击通过、点赞、当然还有 pin、停留时长。我们做这些实验，得到各种不同数据，有的升、有的降。我们到底在优化什么？(00:08:24): 有件非常重要的事，就是要有那种清晰：这是我们产品最重要的动作。一切，我们的新用户引导（NUX）必须导向它。如果用户没做这个，那他们的产品体验就缺了什么。真的要有清晰的认知、确切知道你要选的那个、要继续走下去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One more question along these lines. How do you think about this milestone versus the activation milestone for a new user? Do you find they're often the same? Getting your user to that aha moment-
turns.zh: 沿这条线再一个问题。你怎么看这个新用户里程碑对比激活（activation）里程碑？你觉得它们常是同一个吗？把用户带到那个"啊哈"时刻——

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Versus ongoing?
turns.zh: 对比持续性的？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Right. Part of it is how do you measure the success of your NUX, of the activation? To me, it is are you taking those new users and helping them understand the mental model of your product well enough that they start completing the core action.
turns.zh: 对。部分在于你怎么衡量 NUX、激活的成功。对我来说，是你能否把那些新用户、帮他们理解你产品的心智模型到足够好，让他们开始完成核心动作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: There was a NUCs once that we played with at Pinterest where we didn't even teach people what pinning was. It was their feed magically appeared and it was a real ... That was an example of okay, we have to help people understand that they are here to discover something and save it to their board.
turns.zh: Pinterest 曾有个我们试过的 NUX，我们甚至不教人 pin 是什么。他们的 feed 神奇地出现，那是真的……那是个例子：好，我们得帮人理解他们是来发现东西、并保存到画板的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just in case people don't know what NUX is, new user experience. It's just an acronym for new user experience.
turns.zh: 以防有人不知道 NUX 是什么——新用户体验（new user experience）。它就是新用户体验的缩写。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Thank you. Yes.
turns.zh: 谢谢。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Maybe one more just foundational thing that I think we maybe skipped is what's the best way to think about using this framework? Is this essentially where you should focus your energy, on which elements of your product you should be driving, which metrics to focus on? Is that a simple way to think about ... Basically, we've talked about layer one and there's three layers. What's the best way to think about, as you're talking through this framework, of how to apply it and use it?
turns.zh: 好。也许还有个基础的东西我觉得我们跳过了——用这个框架最好的思考方式是什么？这本质上是不是你该把精力聚焦在哪、驱动产品的哪些元素、聚焦哪些指标？这是想它简单的办法吗？……基本上，我们聊了第一层，共三层。聊到这个框架时，最好的思考方式、如何应用它使用它，是什么？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: In a way, you have to think holistically when you're building these consumer products, when you're designing it. But I think it's very important, once you get the product out and you're starting to optimize, to start thinking through each of the levels. That's just very focusing, to help a founder understand, "What are the levers that I really have to be focusing on to improve?"
turns.zh: 某种意义上，你建这些消费产品、设计它时，得整体地想。但我觉得很重要的一点是，一旦产品出来、你开始优化，就开始逐层思考。那非常聚焦，帮创始人理解"我真正得聚焦哪些杠杆去改进？"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I want to come back to how to apply it, in maybe some examples, after we go through the three levels so I'll turn it back to you.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我想回头聊怎么应用它、也许用些例子，在走过三层之后，所以我把话交还给你。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Perfect. Let's say you're building your product and you're starting to see that you have users completing the core action. Then, the next challenge you have, and I've seen this many times before, is that then you have to figure out how to get those users to stick around. You want to retain those users. Obviously, if they do the core action once or twice, and then they run out of steam, you're going to be in a really challenged position to build something that endures. (00:11:03): The test for me, of whether you're building a product that has the ingredients to create a retentive product on a micro level, just at the user level, is that the product should get better the more you use it, and you'll have more to lose by leaving it. I'll give you a couple examples there, a couple of my favorite products. (00:11:26): Obviously, Pinterest. One of the features that I worked on when I was at Pinterest and we shipped was this idea of a picked for you feed. The idea was every time you pinned something to a board, we would take that information that the user gave us and use it to create recommendations in their home feed. It may have been the first algorithmic feed that was in a social product because, suddenly your home feed wasn't just things and people that you followed. The truth is, people weren't really following other people on Pinterest so we needed a way to make the experience get better the more you used it, so we started to do these recommendations in your home feed. (00:12:10): It was this experience that, the more you pinned, the more personalized your home feed got for you. Then, the more you pinned, you also had more to lose by leaving Pinterest because, all of a sudden, you had all your favorite books, articles you wanted to remember, the recipes that you were planning on cooking one day, the holiday planning that you were doing. So you wouldn't abandon Pinterest because Pinterest was this repository for these different expressions of your identity, or these different bookmarks that you wanted to back to. That was this idea. It's very important that the core action is the thing that you use as the product to make the experience better over time. (00:12:52): Evernote, another example. I don't know if you're an Evernote user.
turns.zh: 完美。假设你建产品，开始看到有用户完成核心动作。然后，你下一个挑战——我见过很多次——是搞清怎么让那些用户留下来。你想留存那些用户。显然，如果他们做一两次核心动作就后继乏力，你建持久东西会很有挑战。(00:11:03): 对我来说，测试你是否在微观层面、用户层面建一个有留存要素的产品，是：产品应该越用越好，而离开它你会损失越多。我给你几个例子，几个我最爱的产品。(00:11:26): 显然，Pinterest。我在 Pinterest 做、并发布的一个功能是"为你精选"（picked for you）feed 的想法。想法是每次你 pin 东西到画板，我们就用用户给我们的信息，在他们的首页 feed 创建推荐。它可能是社交产品里第一个算法 feed，因为突然你的首页 feed 不只是你关注的人和东西。事实是，人们在 Pinterest 不太关注别人，所以我们需要一种方式让体验

turns.en: No. I tried it once and it was way too complicated, and I gave up quickly.
turns.zh: 不。我试过一次，太复杂了，很快放弃。

turns.en: People still laugh at me for being an Evernote user.
turns.zh: 人们还笑我是 Evernote 用户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: I'm a lifetime user.
turns.zh: 我是终身用户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.en: It's one of those things that I take all my notes in Evernote. I dump documents in Evernote. What I means is that, the more I use it ... Now I know that I can do a search in my Evernote and I'm going to find the document I'm looking for. Now, I can never leave Evernote. It has everything. I have thousands and thousands of documents in Evernote. That's a product that's incredibly retentive.
turns.zh: 我是那种把所有笔记、所有文档都丢进 Evernote 的人。意思是，我用得越多……现在我知道我能在 Evernote 里搜到我要的文档。现在，我永远离不开 Evernote。它什么都有。我有成千上万文档在 Evernote。那是个极度留存的产品。

turns.en: Unless someone builds a great exporter, and then there goes that piece of friction.
turns.zh: 除非有人建个超棒的导出器，然后那块摩擦就没了。

turns.en: People keep telling me I need to move on to Notion or something else, but not yet. I will remain a dinosaur here.
turns.zh: 人们一直跟我说我得换到 Notion 或别的，但还没。我会继续当这里的恐龙。

turns.en: Wow. I love that that's an example of someone can break that barrier and make it less retentive, by making it easier to get off.
turns.zh: 哇。我爱那是个例子——有人能打破那道屏障、让留存变低，通过让离开更容易。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting growth strategy, basically.
turns.zh: 那基本是个有意思的增长策略。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Yes. Yeah, it's very true. Let's say, now, you have a product, it's growing, more people are completing the core action. When they complete that core action, the product gets more retentive for them. It gets better the more they use it, they have more to lose by leaving it. Then, your tall task, and this is the hardest thing to overcome, is how do you make the product self-perpetuating? This is where I love to think of every time a user users your product, let's say they're clicking on the mouse or they're tapping on their phone, I love to think of it as this kinetic energy that they're putting into your product. You're taking that energy, and your job with a great product, is to take that energy and, as much as possible, convert it back to the experience that they're having with your product. (00:14:55): Now, the biggest thing that you can do is a network effect. The more I pin something on Pinterest, the better the experience for every user on Pinterest. Every time I add a pin to a board, I'm creating a new edge in Pinterest Graph, that Pinterest then uses to create recommendations and enrich their understanding of all those objects on Pinterest. The network effect is the strongest thing that you can do. And obviously, if you have that, which all social products have to in some way, you have to spend time, as much as possible, just maximizing where that shows up, fine-tuning it, removing friction so that it's a flywheel that spins faster and faster. (00:15:42): But, there's other loops too, that you have to identify and then maximize. These are the growth and re-engagement loops. These are classic loops, you talk about these a lot, they exist in marketplaces and social products. How do you get it so that, as your users use the product, they want to share it with other people? They create metadata that you can then use for SEO. You have collaborative experiences that pull other people in. There's all different things you can do here. And then, there's also things that you can do to re-engage a user. (00:16:18): As an example, in the early days of Pinterest, if you pinned something, you're pinning something that you found on Pinterest that somebody else pinned. So we would send a push notification, "Hey, Lenny, Sarah just pinned your pin to her art board." Now, if you were a dormant user at that point, it's been a couple weeks since you'd used Pinterest, that notification might pull you back into Pinterest and be like, "Hey, I wonder what other pins Sarah has on her art board." It's a great re-engagement loop where Pinterest doesn't have to do anything there intentional. The user is creating the action that drives the outcome that Pinterest wants in that example. (00:17:03): Now, as much as I love Evernote, this is a place where Evernote obviously falls down. There's no loops that they can take advantage of, that when I use the product, I make it better for you. There's no loop where, when I use the product, I want to pull you into the product. They tried at some point, to do collaborative journals, it doesn't work. That's a place where, because of that, Evernote had to spend money to acquire users, they tapped out. They missed that level three. (00:17:38): There's other examples I could speak to, of companies that weren't able to transcend to level three, that you wouldn't otherwise think. I think of companies like Houseparty and Clubhouse. What was interesting about both of those products is that you would think that the more users that came into Clubhouse or Houseparty, the faster the flywheel should spin. But the challenge was that they relied on push notifications. I don't know if you had this experience, but let's take Houseparty as an example. You started to follow a lot of people on Houseparty, and then all of a sudden, your push notifications just got overwhelming. Because it was a realtime product, that you had to use push noti cations to know the moment to join the product, but when you had so many push notifications because the more people you followed, the more notifications you had, you just get to this point where you start ignoring them. It becomes this thing where, even though the flywheel should be spinning faster, it starts breaking down. That's the real tricky nuance in this level three.
turns.zh: 对。对，非常真。假设你现在有个产品，在增长，越来越多人完成核心动作。当他们完成核心动作，产品对他们更留存。越用越好，离开损失越多。然后，你的大任务——这是最难克服的——是怎么让产品自我永续（self-perpetuating）？这是我每次用户用你产品时都爱想的：假设他们在点鼠标或敲手机，我爱把它想成他们注入产品的动能（kinetic energy）。你拿那能量，而好产品的你的工作，是拿那能量、尽可能转化回他们与产品的体验。(00:14:55): 现在，你能做的最大一件事是网络效应。我在 Pinterest 多 pin 一个，每个 Pinterest 用户的体验就更好一点。每次我往画板加一个 pin，我就在 Pinterest 图谱里创造一条新边，Pinterest 用它来创建推荐、丰富它对 Pinterest 上所有对象的理解。网络效应是你能做的最强的事。显然，如果你有它——所有社交产品某种方式都得有——你得尽可能花时间最大化它出现的地方，微调

turns.en: What I often feel is that, a lot of times, product founders, consumer founders, see where they want to get to, they compare themselves to the full expression of a product that you see with other products, ROBLOX, Instagram, TikTok, whatever it may be, and they want to get there. And that's actually part of the importance of understanding level one, what your core action is, is that you want to make sure that when a user comes to your product, signs up for the first time, doesn't have necessarily a lot of contacts on what the product is itself, that they see the thing that they're supposed to do and you get them to do it. (00:31:19): And so, I feel that that's the first mistake, and it's kind of natural that it would be the first mistake, but maybe the largest mistake that I see people make.

(00:34:36): And so, we did this kind of top down, bottoms up analysis to make it very clear that when we launch an experiment or launch a new feature, if the probability, if the percentage of people that pin something doesn't go up, or the number of pins for that cohort doesn't go up, that experiment is not a a successful experiment.

(00:41:46): The other way you could think of it is like if you're trying to get to $1,000,000 of GMV as quickly as possible, you're actually motivated to go after a really big market, right? Basically you're trying to figure out how do you create a engine that continues to drive supply and also drives demand. So a fun example is when Etsy was getting started, as you know, they went to craft fairs and pitched sellers, "Hey, sign up for Etsy. You could sell your stuff online." And then all their sellers started telling all their buyers, "Hey, buy my stuff on Etsy."
turns.zh: 太棒了。我会链到我做市场那篇有很多这些洞察的贴子，但还有几个只是有趣的。基本你在搞清怎么创造一台引擎持续驱动供给侧、也驱动需求侧。所以个好玩的例子是 Etsy 起步时，如你知道，他们去手工艺集市、向卖家推销"嘿，注册 Etsy。你能在线上卖你的东西。"然后所有卖家开始告诉所有买家"嘿，在 Etsy 买我的东西。"

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Etsy literally gave them business cards. So Etsy gave their sellers business cards that made them feel like, "Oh, I'm a real..." Made them feel professional. And the link on it was to their Etsy store.
turns.zh: Etsy 真的给了他们名片。所以 Etsy 给卖家名片，让他们感觉"哦，我是个真的……"让他们感觉专业。上面的链接指向他们的 Etsy 店。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. One of the most magical growth engines of marketplaces is when your supply brings on the demand. So that's a really good example. Another one is DoorDash, where basically a restaurant signed up for DoorDash and then they tell all the customers, "You want to order our food? Go to DoorDash and order it." And so all the restaurants are telling everyone about DoorDash and then they become DoorDash users and they order from other restaurants.
turns.zh: 我爱那个。市场最神奇的增长引擎之一，是你的供给侧带来需求侧。所以那是好例子。另一个是 DoorDash，基本一个餐厅注册了 DoorDash，然后他们告诉所有顾客"你想点我们的食物？去 DoorDash 点。"所以所有餐厅都在跟所有人说 DoorDash，然后他们成了 DoorDash 用户、从其他餐厅点。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Yes, and it shows how creative DoorDash was to both sides of the market in that example.
turns.zh: 对，它显示了 DoorDash 对市场两边都多创意，在那个例子里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then Faire is an awesome example too. It sounds similar to REKKI as you described, where Faire is basically a B2B artisanal items marketplace where boutique shops buy nice candles and blankets for their store to sell. And essentially they did what you described, where they signed on a store and they basically told them, "All your vendors can join for free and not have to pay any fees if they sign up for Faire, and it makes it easy for you to buy their stuff." And then on the other side, a candlemaker tells all the places they sell to, "Hey, you should use Faire. It's so easy to buy our stuff, and we can communicate through there." And they can sign up without any fees. So basically everyone just invites all their existing partners on Faire, and then everyone's on Faire. So yeah, there's a lot of ways to do it.
turns.zh: 然后 Faire 也是超棒例子。它听起来像你描述的 REKKI，Faire 基本是个 B2B 手工艺品市场，精品店为他们的店买好蜡烛和毯子来卖。本质他们做了你描述的，他们签下一家店，基本告诉他们"你所有供应商都能免费加入、如果注册 Faire 不用付任何费，而且让你容易买他们的东西。"然后另一边，一个蜡烛匠告诉所有他们卖去的地方"嘿，你该用 Faire。买我们的东西太容易了，我们能通过那沟通。"他们能无费注册。所以基本人人都邀他们所有现有伙伴上 Faire，然后人人都在 Faire。所以，有很多办法做。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: I love it. And so the second type of loop, and again this loop works symbiotically with the growth loop, is what I call happiness loops. And I think of them almost as the kidneys for your marketplace as you grow. The happiness loop, the idea is you have a lot of new sellers coming in, and of course you have new buyers, but you want to make sure that you are matching your buyers with the sellers that are going to give them the best experience. (01:08:23): And so, normally in a consumer social product, churn is heartbreaking. Once a user churns, they're almost never going to come back. And with a consumer social product, you're trying to get to massive scale. But when you're building a marketplace, actually, there's a healthy amount of churn that you want on the supplier side because there are just going to be suppliers who aren't going to create a great experience for the buyer, and you can't do anything about that. (01:08:53): And so we've all had the Uber driver who you give one star to. That person you don't want on your marketplace getting matched with buyers. And so you're trying to then make sure that, as you grow, you have a natural mechanism in your marketplace to reward the suppliers that you want to reward and to churn out the ones that you don't. Of course your job is to do your best to set all the sellers up for success, but it's an inevitability. (01:09:24): And so there's two great examples I think of in these happiness loops, which is around search ranking, and then reputation. Search ranking is just a very obvious one, which is, you're trying to understand what creates a happy experience for the buy side, and then reward the sellers that provide that experience. (01:09:47): So I think an interesting example that ended up actually changing but still is illustrative, is that UberEats in the very beginning of their journey, thought that their advantage in the market was going to be about having really fast delivery, right? Because they already had this network of drivers and so they thought that that's where they were going to really lean in and have an edge over any competition. And so in the search ranking, they rewarded restaurants that prepared the food quickly, and so answered the Uber Eats request, and then actually got the food out as fast as possible so that Uber Eats became synonymous with the quickness by which you got the delivery. And so that restaurant that takes 40 minutes to prepare the food, they would get ranked low in the experience for Uber Eats, even if the food was really, really great.
turns.zh: 我爱。那么这第二类循环，again 这循环和增长循环共生，是我所谓的快乐循环（happiness loops）。我把它们想成你增长时市场的"肾脏"。快乐循环的想法是，你有好多新卖家进来，当然也有新买家，但你想确保你把买家匹配给那些会给他们最好体验的卖家。(01:08:23): 所以，通常在消费社交产品，流失（churn）是心碎的。一旦用户流失，他们几乎从不回来。而消费社交产品你想到巨大规模。但当你建市场，其实供给侧有健康量的流失是你想要的，因为就是会有不能给买家好体验的供应商，你对此无能为力。(01:08:53): 所以我们都有过那个给一星的 Uber 司机。那人不该在你的市场被匹配给买家。所以你试图确保，随你增长，你的市场有自然机制奖励你想奖励的卖家、淘汰你不想的。当然你的工作是尽力让所有卖家成功，但那是必然。(01:09:24): 所以

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so we've been talking about tipping of the marketplace. Is there anything else there that you want to share before we move on to the third layer?
turns.zh: 好，我们聊了市场倾斜。转第三层前还有没有别的想分享？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Yeah, there's two other things that come to mind. One, just as a reminder, and then one as a caution. So the reminder is in order to tip a market, you have to reach a saturation point in that market. You can't tip a market before you've penetrated it to some saturation level. And it goes back to level one of why you want to focus on a constrained market. (01:11:23): Let's take growing a food delivery product in Des Moines, Iowa versus LA or New York. When you're growing in a small city and you're focused on restaurants, you're going to be able to get to this tipping point a lot faster and more efficiently than if you're going after a very big market. And so there's a real advantage to being able to prove out the playbook as quickly as possible and as efficiently as possible before you move on to bigger challenges. And so I think it underscores, again, why it's so valuable in the beginning to focus on something that is constrained. (01:12:09): And again, Postmates focusing on San Francisco, the city. DoorDash focusing initially on the suburbs, much smaller opportunity, but one that they could really knock the cover off the ball on. They had no competition. They had a customer that was desperate for attention, and so they could make them happy. And that just sets you up for real success to go from strength to the adjacent market. (01:12:38): The second thing that I'd say is, and this is so important is that not all markets are susceptible to tipping, right? We've all experienced this, I'm sure Lenny, with the companies that you work with, the companies I work with, where there are conditions of a market that make it vulnerable to tipping. I have six in my post just to name a couple classic ones. (01:13:11): The first obvious one is just concentration on the supply side. In order to be able to tip a market, you need suppliers to want to lean in on your marketplace. My partner, Bill Gurley talks about how great marketplaces create the new incumbents. So you basically have suppliers who aren't the incumbents. The incumbents aren't going to lean in on your marketplace, they're already fat and happy, but you want to have these hungry suppliers who lean in. But if there's already concentration in your marketplace, in the ecosystem, the market that you're playing in, then you're not going to have sellers lean in, and you're not going to be able to create a flywheel that spins where the more sellers you bring on, the better the pricing or experiences on the demand side because the sellers are happy and there's nobody that's hungry or fighting. And so that's just a critical, critical point.
turns.zh: 对，还有两件想到的事。一个提醒，一个警示。提醒是，要倾斜一个市场，你得在那个市场达到饱和点。你不能在渗透到一个饱和水平前倾斜它。那回到第一层——为什么你想聚焦受限市场。(01:11:23): 拿在 Des Moines、Iowa 增长食物配送产品 vs LA 或纽约。你在小城市、聚焦餐厅时，会比追大市场快得多、高效多地到达临界点。所以真有优势：尽快、高效证明打法，再走向更大挑战。所以我觉得 again 强调，开始聚焦受限东西多值。(01:12:09): Again，Postmates 聚焦 San Francisco 这城市。DoorDash 最初聚焦郊区，机会小得多，但他们能彻底击球出击。他们没竞争。他们有急需关注的顾客，所以他们能让人开心。那只是为你从优势到相邻市场设好真正的成功。(01:12:38): 我要说的第二件事，而且

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Bill Gurley and I actually had a little Twitter debate once about supply versus demand and which one's more important. And basically his pitch was like, "All that really matters in the end, to build a successful marketplace, is can you find the demand? Can you bring the demand to your marketplace?" It makes all the sense in the world. Everything in the end is, "Can you find customers?" (01:14:34): In the work I've done looking into marketplaces, what I find is the hardest thing to do, to bring people to your marketplace, is to find the supply and bring it to people, basically aggregate it. And your point here is exactly right, is that basically the value of your marketplace is to find this non-concentrated demand that's all over the place and bring it together and make it easy to transact with. So I think that is really important, just to double down on this point, that what makes the marketplace valuable is supply that is hard to find that you make easy to find and transact with. And I feel like that's almost the core of what makes marketplace work.
turns.zh: Bill Gurley 和我其实有次小 Twitter 辩论，关于供给侧 vs 需求侧哪个更重要。基本他的论点是"最终真正重要的，建成功市场，是你能找到需求吗？你能把需求带到你的市场吗？"那完全说得通。最终一切是"你能找到客户吗？"(01:14:34): 在我做的研究看市场，我发现最难的事、把人带到你市场，是找供给侧并带给人们、基本聚合它。你的点在这完全对——市场的价值是找这种分散在各处、非集中的需求，把它聚起来、让交易变容易。所以我觉得那真重要，就强调这点：让市场有价值的，是难找、你让它易找易交易的供给侧。我觉得那几乎是市场能工作的核心。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: I think you're both right.
turns.zh: 我觉得你们都对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I think we're both right. Right, right.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得我们都对。对，对。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Because in the beginning, the only way you get started with the marketplace, obviously, is you're bringing the supply online, and that's what opens up the opportunity. And the only way then for you to have a chance at tipping the market is if there's enough fragmentation on the supply side to create a differentiated experience for the demand side to care about your marketplace. But the only way to build long-term enduring value with a marketplace is to corner the demand side. And so it's kind of a little bit that evolution of a marketplace that ends up changing who you focus on. (01:15:55): And I don't know if you've experienced this in my experience with the marketplaces that I work with, it's a constant like, "I have to focus more on the demand side right now. Okay, now we got to focus more on the supply side." And it's just back to how difficult these businesses are to build, especially when you have limited resources, that it's like the forever battle of building a marketplace.
turns.zh: 因为开始，唯一启动市场的方式，显然，是你把供给侧上线，那才打开机会。而你有机会倾斜市场的唯一方式，是供给侧有足够碎片化、能为需求侧创造差异化体验、让他们 care 你的市场。但建长期持久价值的唯一方式，是圈住需求侧。所以那有点是市场的演化，最终改变你聚焦谁。(01:15:55): 我不知道你经验里有没有，我和合作的市场，常是"我现在得更聚焦需求侧。好，现在得更聚焦供给侧。"那只是回到这些生意多难建，尤其资源有限时，像建市场的永恒战斗。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, especially if it's a geographically oriented marketplace like a DoorDash. Sometimes you have more customers than restaurants.
turns.zh: 对，尤其如果是像 DoorDash 这种偏地理的市场。有时你顾客比餐厅多。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sometimes you have too many restaurants, not enough customers.
turns.zh: 有时你餐厅太多、顾客不够。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, it's very city dependent. At Airbnb we had basically many attempts at a dashboard of which market is supply constrained, which is demand constrained. Along the same lines, I think it's also something I think about with B2B marketplaces, the reason they're challenging, in my experience, to work, there's so few of them, is the supply is rarely fragmented. Usually there are very few suppliers, so it's pretty easy. "I'm just going to pick one of these 10 and I don't need you." Is that true? Is that how you think about the challenges of B2B marketplaces?
turns.zh: 所以，非常取决于城市。在 Airbnb 我们有基本很多次尝试做仪表盘，看哪个市场供给侧约束、哪个需求侧约束。沿同样线，我觉得也是我思考 B2B 市场时、我的经验里它们挑战的原因——它们这么少——供给侧很少碎片化。通常供应商极少，所以挺容易。"我就挑这 10 个里的一个，我不需要你。"是真的吗？你这么想 B2B 市场的挑战吗？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: There's definitely that, but I think actually the bigger challenge with B2B marketplaces is on the homogeneity of the supply. When you think about a lot of labor marketplaces, and let's take a classic example of Mechanical Turk, right? What you need in a marketplace for that flywheel... I have a graph in my slides where you show that the more you penetrate the market, the happier you're able to make your customer. You should have an exponential experience where the flywheel doesn't slow down. Now you take Airbnb as an example, there isn't a limit to how valuable it is to have more supply on Airbnb because everybody has their own special preferences. And there probably is a theoretical limit, but you just feel like there is always going to be the, there's such heterogeneity in the supply for Airbnb, that that's what has let Airbnb really close and escape competition. (01:18:04): With B2B marketplaces what sometimes happens, like a labor marketplace, is that you have this homogeneity in the supply, where it's not clear that adding the next incremental unit of supply actually changes the experience for the demand side. And so at Mechanical Turk, whether Mechanical Turk has a hundred thousand Turkers or 5 million Turkers, it probably doesn't really change the experience for somebody who is using Mechanical Turk. And that's why in the early days, a Mechanical Turk, you saw a lot of other copycats or clones of Mechanical Turk doing something similar because it didn't take that much supply for them to be able to create an experience for a segment of the market that was as good as the already scaled Mechanical Turk.
turns.zh: 确实有那点，但我觉得其实 B2B 市场更大的挑战是供给侧的同质性（homogeneity）。当你想很多劳动力市场，经典例子 Mechanical Turk，对吧？市场里那飞轮需要的……我幻灯片里有个图显示你渗透市场越多，你能让客户越开心。你该有指数级体验，飞轮不减速。拿 Airbnb 为例，更多供给侧的价值没有上限，因为人人有自己特殊偏好。也许有理论上限，但你感觉总有、Airbnb 供给侧如此异质（heterogeneity），那正是让 Airbnb 真正关上、逃开竞争。(01:18:04): 用 B2B 市场有时发生的，像劳动力市场，是你有供给侧同质性，不清楚加下一个增量供给侧单位是否真改变需求侧体验。所以在 Mechanical Turk，无论它有十万还是五百万 Turkers，对用 Mechanical Turk 的人大概不改变体验。那也是为什么早期，Mechanical Turk 你看到很多

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I'm glad we got into that. We're getting real dirty about marketplaces. Exactly what I was hoping for. You said that you had something else you wanted to share along these lines.
turns.zh: 太棒了。高兴我们聊到那。我们在市场里挖得很深。正是我希望的。你说还有别的想分享沿这条线。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: And there's so many other examples of reasons why a marketplace won't tip competition. Again, you're a food delivery company and you go after the suburbs where there's no competition. That makes your job really easy to tip the market. You go to New York City where you have an entrenched competitor of Grubhub plus Seamless Web, a different culture around delivery where the restaurants mostly have their own delivery fleets, and it's just going to be so much harder for you to tip that market. And so, I think you have to be really context aware when you're building a marketplace of what your competition's going to be so that you see if there is a path for you to actually tip the market.
turns.zh: 而太多别的原因市场不会倾斜竞争。Again，你是食物配送公司、去没竞争的郊区。那让你的活倾斜市场很容易。你去纽约市，有根深蒂固的竞争者 Grubhub 加 Seamless Web、围绕配送的不同文化——餐厅大多有自己的配送队，那对你倾斜那市场会难太多。所以，我觉得建市场时你得真正有语境意识：你的竞争会是什么，看你是否有路径真倾斜市场。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And even if you've tipped the market, it may get untipped, like Uber comes in and starts to eat your lunch, no pun intended. It doesn't last forever. You have to keep fighting for it.
turns.zh: 而即使你倾斜了市场，它可能"解除倾斜"（untipped），像 Uber 进来开始吃你的午餐，没有双关。它不永远持续。你得一直为它战。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Well, and it's such an important point, which is that you can never rest on your laurels when you're building a marketplace. The history of places is one in which you have a marketplace that feels dominant and then gets disrupted by a competitor. HomeAway, VRBO being disrupted by the likes of you at Airbnb.
turns.zh: 嗯，那是如此重要的点——建市场时你永不能躺在功劳簿上。地方的历史是：你有个感觉统治的市场、然后被竞争者颠覆。HomeAway、VRBO 被你这样的 Airbnb 颠覆。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I wish I could take credit for all that. Yeah, so one way I think about it is you're talking about this idea of tipping is, a simple way to think about if tipping is happening, if you're tipping it successfully, is percentage of your growth that's starting to come from organic word of mouth, people just becoming like, "This is the default way I'm going to order food, travel, book a ride."
turns.zh: 我希望我能领那个功。对，所以一种我想它的方式，你聊这倾斜想法——想它简单的办法，倾斜是否发生、你是否成功倾斜它，是你增长中开始来自有机口碑的百分比，人们开始变成"这是我要点餐、旅行、叫车的默认方式。"

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: I think you see two things. You see one, the cohorts getting better. So people start using you more. As the supply side gets more diverse, you have more and more use cases that you start to be able to serve. And so you get the demand side leaning in more, the cohorts get better. And then to your point, you have the organic growth that happens where you don't have to fight to get each new participant on both sides of your market. There's something that starts to happen where the value proposition is just so strong relative to any other substitute that the market starts coming to you.
turns.zh: 我觉得你看两件事。你看一，同期群变好。所以人开始更多用你。随供给侧更多样，你有越来越多能服务的用例。所以需求侧更倾斜向你，同期群变好。然后到你点，你有发生的有机增长，你不必为每个新参与者两边战。有某事开始发生——相对任何替代品，价值主张如此强，市场开始来找你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So essentially, cohort retention starts going up because more and more valuable, and more people are coming to you, just word of mouth or through some loops that you built.
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以本质是，同期群留存开始升，因为更有价值，更多人来找你，就口碑或通过你建的一些循环。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 正是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Anything else on this layer/level of the [inaudible 01:21:41] before?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这层还有别的吗[听不清 01:21:41]之前？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 没。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. Let's talk about dominating the marketplace and what that looks like, and how you do that. How do you dominate a marketplace and win, Sarah Tavel?
turns.zh: 好，酷。让我们聊统治市场（dominating the marketplace）和它什么样、你怎么做到。你怎么统治市场、取胜，Sarah Tavel？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: So yes, level three, and this is the one I feel like every founder who starts a marketplace, they're chomping at the bit to be able to really focus now on growth. Because all along, I feel like we've been holding you back of just, "Focus, focus, focus." And what you're doing through level one and level two as you're honing what you're building, is that you're basically building a playbook. You don't yet know whether this playbook is repeatable. It's not always the case that the dynamics of one market is the same elsewhere. I'll take REKKI as an example. In the London food scene, there's significant fragmentation of suppliers. In the Berlin food scene, that's not the case. And so it's not always the case that whatever you did in one market works in another market, but usually there's something that rhymes. There's a hint of what is going to work. (01:22:56): So what happens now is you have a market that's tipping, and the question then is, are you ready to take your eye off the ball and start to diffuse your focus into other markets? So there's kind of three vectors then that any marketplace can grow at this point. (01:23:17): The first vector is within the existing market where you already are tipping that market. You as a founder then have to make a very personal decision, that what you're looking at is the context of your competitive situation. So if you're tipping a market and you have no other competitor going after that market, you're the first one to see this opportunity, then I think you have two things that you want to do at the same time to grow. (01:23:49): The first thing is that you want to take the existing market that you're in and you just keep doing what you're doing, and you may even find ways to stretch beyond that initial market that you're going after-
turns.zh: 所以，第三层，这是我觉得每个开始市场的创始人，都急不可耐想真聚焦增长了。因为一路以来，我觉得我们一直拉着你"聚焦、聚焦、聚焦。"而你通过第一二层打磨你建的，基本是在建一本打法（playbook）。你还不知道这打法是否可重复。一个市场的动态不总在别处一样。我拿 REKKI 为例。伦敦食物圈，供应商显著碎片化。柏林食物圈，不是那样。所以不总是一个市场做的在另一市场工作，但通常有押韵的东西。有将工作的暗示。(01:22:56): 所以现在发生的是你有个在倾斜的市场，问题于是是，你准备好把眼移开球、开始把焦点扩散到其他市场吗？所以有三向量，任何市场此时能增长。(01:23:17): 第一向量是在你已在倾斜的现有市场内。你作为创始人得做个很个人的决定，你看的是你竞争情境的语境。所以如果你倾斜一个市场

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: ... Beyond that initial market that you're going after, within the same market. And so, what I mean by that is Uber went from black cars to UberX to UberPool. And then, the third vector of growth is you want to then try to get as many plates spinning in as many markets that you can handle as quickly as possible. And this is like the blitz scale, right? This is the land grab. And again, your equity value that you're going to create is going to come from dominating the market. (01:24:59): And so you don't want to plant a thousand flags in a thousand markets at the same time, spread yourself too thin, and not decidedly win any one market. You always want to put more wood behind fewer arrows. The more scale that you have, the more cities or categories where you have the flywheel starting to spin and you're starting to see the tipping point happen, the stronger your company will be. Each market that you get, you have scale in, where you'll have contribution profit. You take that contribution profit, you invest it in new markets. The more markets and contribution profit you have, the more venture capital you'll be able to raise, which you then reinvest in growing. And so, this is really the place where you are, as aggressively as possible, while, at the same time, not losing sight of the fact that your goal is, in each market individually, to dominate that market, you're trying to grow into as much possible market opportunity as you possibly can.
turns.zh: ……超越你追的初始市场，在同一市场内。所以我的意思是 Uber 从黑车到 UberX 到 UberPool。他们在已统治的地理里一直找办法、通过扩展服务的用例一直变强。所以你持续生长和渗透市场，找办法回答那市场里你能做的更多用例，尤其如果你没很多竞争。然后，第三增长向量是你然后想尽快让尽量多的盘子在尽量多的市场转。而这就像 blitz scale，对吧？这是圈地（land grab）。Again，你要创造的股权价值将来自统治市场。(01:24:59): 所以你不想同时在千个市场插千面旗、把自己摊太薄、没决定性赢任何一市场。你总想"更少箭后放更多木"（put more wood behind fewer arrows）。你规模越大、有飞轮开始转的城市或品类越多、你开始看到临界点发生，你公司越强。每个你拿到、有规模的市场，你有贡献利润（contribution profit）。你拿那贡献利润，投到新市场。越多市场和贡献

turns.zh: Again，这重要的原因是大多有野心的创始人从这开始。他们就"立即做大、blitz scale。我们得在任何人追上前来得快赢。"所以，again，提醒那是最后一步，一旦你做了前两步。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel

You have a competitor come in, and guess what? They put a million dollars into one city, they're going to win that city, and that's going to set them up for greater success down the road, to keep on being able to get more capital and more expense that they can put to work to grow those cities. And of course, we never have one competitor. Always have a lot of competitors. And so, focus on these steps is just, it really is such an important thing to have discipline around.
turns.zh: 对，那是如此重要的点，因为别忘了，你永远脆弱于竞争。所以，假设你有 100 万，你把那 100 万 go-to-market 成本摊在 10 城市，摊太薄。你有竞争者进来，猜怎么着？他们把 100 万投进一城市，他们会赢那城市，那为他们设好未来更大成功，能继续拿更多资本、更多费用投到那些城市生长。当然，我们从不只一个竞争者。总很多竞争者。所以，聚焦这些步骤就是，有纪律围绕它真重要。

turns.zh: 所以你仍能建好生意，即使你不统治、统治。只是你不会赚那么多钱，近乎那么多利润，基本你的现金流。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Something that you all at Benchmark are really big on, which I think would be interesting to talk about, is the TAM not being as big a deal as people think. turns.zh: Benchmark 你们全都很大力的，我觉得有意思聊的，是 TAM 没人们想的那么大事。所以很多时候，很多市场起步很小，有恐惧市场就是不够大、长期建不了大生意。而你们不那么在乎，不像很多其他投资人，市场本身不是投资的大杀手。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: I would underline it even, which is that we get excited about the markets, the opportunities, that might seem small from the outside.

turns.en: I love it. Can you speak to that and help people understand [inaudible 01:29:10]?

turns.zh: 对，但你听说过，Etsy 也低估了年年年。Hipcamp，让我们兴奋的部分就是它是个其实比外人想的大得多的市场。而追这些被低估市场的妙处是，它们开始没竞争。所以，你有更多元素能运作进一个市场、把市场倾斜向你，当你没竞争时。所以，我们爱这类市场，我们总对外面的创始人说，如果别人告诉你市场太小，我们很想认识你。

(01:31:34): And so, what happened with Hipcamp is that, in the beginning, it was going after this very different market segment, but as they became successful, made their landowners money, those landowners invested that money back into their land and started to open up the market opportunity for Hipcamp, into people more like me, that are glampers, that want that experience in nature, but maybe don't want to pitch a tent to have it. turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel

We could talk about currents later, if we want to, but that there's something that's creating momentum in the market, that's opening up an opportunity for this marketplace to exist. And for whatever reason, that founder is the person who sees it. And it's kind of one of those things that, once you see it, you're like, "How does it still work this way?" (01:35:01): And it's kind of back to focusing their ambition, like a laser beam, as opposed to this broad sun trying to do everything. turns.zh: 有几件事。一是，我其实想一个最近见的创始人，那里有那"赚来的秘密"（earned secret），他们看到一个别人忽视、没被解决的市场机会。也许过去有原因没被解决，但现在就是时刻，有某事在变、在市场创造一股洋流。我们以后聊洋流，如果愿意，但那有在市场创造动量、打开这市场存在机会的东西。而无论为何，那创始人是看到它的人。那有点像一旦你看到，你就"这怎么还这样工作？"而有人进来做点什么太说得通了。然后，第二件总是深深共鸣、此时明显为何真是那样的事，是真正有聚焦的创始人。(01:35:01): 而那回到把他们野心像激光束聚焦，而非这 broad 太阳想做一切。所以你真感觉他们聚焦对的事，而那其实导向第三件事，你真感觉，当创始人要么试图用虚荣指标骗你或骗自己，vs 真正的理智诚实和理智严谨——"我的生意里什么真工作？什么不工作？我们聚焦在哪让它尽所能好？"而老兄，那总是，那是你建长期持久价值的方式，而我觉得它贯穿我有幸合作的所有创始人。

"I'm building a marketplace and I need to think of everything," from this marketplace perspective versus 95% of your challenges, questions, hurdles are going to be just whatever startup has to deal with. turns.zh: 我爱这答案的一点是我常关于市场说的——你大多问题不是市场问题或疑问。就是每个初创得处理的。所以你分享的本质是个"赚来的秘密"，适用于任何生意，也许浮现你能乘的浪里的洋流，有很好的聚焦、也聚焦对指标。我 100% 同意。而也有意思，它可能是市场、可能不是，我觉得人们常过重估"我在建市场、我得从市场视角想一切" vs 你 95% 的挑战、疑问、障碍会是任何初创得处理的。然后，有一点市场特有。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: And I want to just double click on the current thing, because it's very related, which is a lot of people, and this is back to maybe our contrarian take on markets, I think a lot of people think about markets almost like these bodies of water. And I actually think that the most interesting markets, you have to think of them like currents, where there's something happening in the market that's creating this current, where you can have a plank of wood that you've put on the river and it's going to pull you forward, versus a market that doesn't really have that momentum to it, you're going to have to build something really big and fancy to make any progress. And that's why we care less about market size, because really, what you're looking for when you're looking at a market are what are the dynamics of change, what's the current and momentum that's going to pull the company and make the job easier for the founders to actually build something that endures?
turns.zh: 我想就"洋流"这事双击，因为它很相关——很多人，回到也许我们对市场的反共识看法，我觉得很多人想市场像这些水体。像"哦，是我们去追的大片水域。"而我其实觉得最有趣的市场，你得想成洋流——市场里正发生什么、创造这股洋流，让你放块木板在河上、它拉你向前，vs 没那势能的市场，你得建又大又花哨的东西才能进展。那正是我们不太在乎市场规模的原因——真，你看市场时找的，是变化的动力、是那股会拉公司向前、让创始人更容易建持久东西的洋流和动量？

turns.en: Essentially, "Why now?" is how a lot of people think about this, right?
turns.zh: 本质"为什么是现在？"（Why now?）是很多人想这个的方式，对吧？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Yes, yes.
turns.zh: 对，对。

turns.en: I love just the visual of a current. There's a startup I invested in, as an example of the opposite, that's a crypto marketplace sort of thing. turns.zh: 我爱洋流的画面。有个我投的初创，作为反例，是个 crypto 市场类的东西。他们在 crypto 很火时起步，并在 crypto 冬天浮现时继续建。他们就意识到"我们的时机，这不是建 crypto 公司的时候，那是新的、试图和已有的竞争。"所以，那是个例子……你得认出当浪朝反方向、一切把你拉离成功。你描述的相反。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Yes. I might have a nuance there, because I think crypto is too broad of a way to describe it. If you said it was a DeFi crypto company, then yes, definitely, with treasuries where they are, the opportunity in DeFi isn't as material as it once was, which stablecoins, I'm a huge believer in stablecoins, and I think that's a market where we have a real current. With inflation and so many local currencies, there's real demand for stablecoins, the US dollar stablecoin, that comes in many different shapes and forms, that is something that I believe has a very strong current right now, that I'm actually quite excited about.
turns.zh: 对。我也许有点细微差别，因为我觉得 crypto 描述太宽。如果你说它是 DeFi crypto 公司，那对，绝对，以国债现在的状况，DeFi 的机会没以前实质，而稳定币（stablecoins），我是稳定币的大信徒，我觉得那是有真洋流的市场。有通胀和那么多本地货币，对稳定币、美元稳定币有真需求，以很多不同形态，那是我觉得现在很有强洋流的、我其实挺兴奋的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, interesting. Yeah, I should have been clear. It's like a very specific part of crypto that's just not happening too much, versus what it was. Okay, we've gone totally off track. So let me come back to our track and see what else you wanted to share around the hierarchy of marketplaces either on the top...
turns.zh: 哦，有趣。对，我该清楚。是 crypto 里非常具体、现在没怎么发生的一部分，vs 它以前。好，我们完全跑题了。让我回轨道、看你想就市场层级分享的其他、在顶层……

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: That's it.
turns.zh: 就那些。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. We did it. Amazing.
turns.zh: 好。我们做到了。惊人。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have a couple more questions sort of related, but I guess, is there anything else that you wanted to say about the hierarchy of marketplaces?
turns.zh: 我有几个相关问题，但我猜，关于市场层级还有别的你想说的吗？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Maybe just this kind of the coda, which is like you can never rest on your laurels, and we talked about this already, but the history of marketplaces is one of disruption. And the idea with happiness is that, and Amazon and Bezos talk about this, which is expectations, consumer expectations, are constantly going up. And so, if you ever stagnate in the experience that you give to the consumer, guess what? You're going to get disrupted. And the examples of we talked about with Airbnb and HomeAway, DoorDash, and Grubhub, Grubhub wasn't able to, for different reasons, they were a public company, and so, they couldn't access capital in the same way that the private markets could. But they were too slow to change the atomic unit of their supply to have delivery that they fulfilled. And so, they got disrupted by the DoorDash, Uber Eats of the world. And so, you just can't rest on your laurels. Expectations constantly go up. And it's part of what's so exciting about this market that we play in.
turns.zh: 也许就这尾声（coda），就是永远不能躺在功劳簿上，我们聊过，但市场的历史是颠覆的历史。而快乐这想法，Amazon 和 Bezos 聊这个，消费者期望在不断上升。所以，如果你在给消费者的体验上停滞，猜怎么着？你会被颠覆。我们聊的 Airbnb 和 HomeAway、DoorDash 和 Grubhub 例子，Grubhub 因不同原因没能——他们是上市公司，所以没法像私募市场那样拿资本。但他们太慢改变他们供给侧的原子单元（atomic unit）去有他们履约的配送。所以，他们被 DoorDash、Uber Eats 之流颠覆。所以，你就是不能躺在功劳簿上。期望不断上升。而那是我们玩的市场如此令人兴奋的一部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think Grubhub is a great example of that, where they were the first really successful food delivery company, and then, even with network effects, by far, the best way to order. And then, DoorDash comes around and wins, because they go bigger and spend a lot of money that Grubhub wasn't willing to spend. Awesome. So I guess the advice there is just don't take for granted your success, even if you have amazing network effects.
turns.zh: 我觉得 Grubhub 是好例子，他们是最早真正成功的食物配送公司，然后即使有网络效应，是远最好的点单方式。然后 DoorDash 出现并赢，因为他们更大、花很多 Grubhub 不愿花的钱。太棒了。所以那的建议就是别把成功当理所当然，即使你有惊人网络效应。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So as we were chatting about this conversation, something you mentioned is that, even if you're not building a marketplace, these lessons are actually still useful. So say you're building an open source product or a social network or even a SaaS startup, a lot of these sort of lessons can still apply. What advice would you have for people that have heard what you just shared, but aren't necessarily building a marketplace? What are some of the takeaways as well?
turns.zh: 好。我们聊这对话时，你提过，即使你不是在建市场，这些教训其实仍有用。所以假设你建开源产品、社交网络、甚至 SaaS 初创，很多这类教训仍适用。对听过你刚分享、但不一定在建市场的人，你有什么建议？一些收获是什么？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: At Benchmark, I'm lucky that I have partners who look at very different types of companies that I look at, and we meet such a incredible breadth of founders. And what you just realize, again and again, is that these same lessons hold. With open source, it's about solving a specific developer's need in the beginning and solving it really freaking well, and then, expanding from there. With SaaS, I think maybe the fascinating exception, kind of similar to your Thumbtack exception, I think what Parker Conrad's doing with Rippling and this idea of a compound startup is very different. And actually, he has a level of ambition that is both the sun and a laser at the same time. And so, that's kind of, in a rare founder, you can have that level of execution, but again and again, what you see, and I think a lot of this, for new companies leveraging large language models to build products, is that focus on a constrained market to start is the way to win.
turns.zh: 在 Benchmark，我幸运有看很不同类型公司的合伙人，我们见如此广的创始人。而你刚意识到，again and again，是同样的教训成立。用开源，是开始解决一个特定开发者的需要、并解决得超好，然后从那扩展。用 SaaS，我觉得也许迷人的例外，有点像你 Thumbtack 例外，我觉得 Parker Conrad 用 Rippling 和"复合初创"（compound startup）想法做的非常不同。而其实，他有种既是太阳又是激光的野心。所以，在稀有创始人，你能有那种执行水平，但 again and again，你看到的，我觉得很多这个——用大语言模型建产品的公司——开始聚焦受限市场是取胜之道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that. Basically, it's happy developer in the case of DevTools or happy enterprise user, just get happy people using your product and coming back to it. So I love that as a reminder. One other question is you wrote this post on finding white space in building marketplace, basically someone that wants to build a marketplace, trying to figure out, where is there an opportunity for new marketplace? Do you have any advice for people, say, founders, potential founders, that are looking for ideas and opportunities to build a marketplace for how to find one? Where do you think there's opportunity?
turns.zh: 我爱那个。基本，是 DevTools 情况里的快乐开发者、或快乐企业用户，就让人快乐地用你产品并回来。所以我爱那作为提醒。另一个问题，你写了这篇找市场"空白"（white space）的贴子，基本某人想建市场、试图搞清新市场机会在哪。你对找想法、机会建市场的人——创始人、潜在创始人——有建议吗？你觉得机会在哪？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: It's kind of fun to ask the question whether LLMs change the game or open up new surface area. So in my post, I write about three ways that you can look for a new opportunity. I think it was like, number one, you always find a horizontal marketplace and you find the kind of low NPS part of that segment and you create a marketplace around that. eBay, being a horizontal marketplace, the sneakers being a low NPS part of that, and you get GOAT. The second is finding a niche that no one else is paying attention to. And the Etsy examples we gave, the Hipcamp stories, and bringing that online, taking friction away, and showing that it's actually a bigger market than you think. And then, the third is changing the atomic unit of the supply. So that kind of like Grubhub, the atomic unit there was a restaurant that has its own delivery fleet, and then, Postmates, DoorDash, Uber Eats came in and said, "Actually, it's any restaurant, we'll provide the delivery fleet." (01:44:15): And so, they opened up the available supply. Now, when I think about LLMs, I think there's a real opportunity for the third one. LLMs may make it possible to bring on a supply type that maybe the long tail, that was just, it was too much effort to reach out to them, onboard them, but maybe if you automate that work, you actually create an opportunity to expand the supply in a way that none of us can anticipate right now. And then, who knows whether there's an opportunity with LLMs to create a better experience in one of these kind of low NPS segments of a market or a niche market itself, that makes it possible to bring it online. So I haven't seen anything yet, but I am definitely on the hunt.
turns.zh: 问 LLM 是否改变游戏、打开新面，挺好玩。所以在我的贴子，我写三种找新机会的方式。我觉得像，第一，你总找一个水平市场（horizontal marketplace）、找那细分里低 NPS 的部分、围绕它建市场。eBay 是水平市场，运动鞋是那的低 NPS 部分，你得到 GOAT。第二是找没人注意的 niche。我们给的 Etsy 例子、Hipcamp 故事，把它线上化、移除摩擦、显示它其实比你想的大。第三是改变供给侧的原子单元。所以像 Grubhub，那的原子单元是有自己配送队的餐厅，然后 Postmates、DoorDash、Uber Eats 进来"其实，是任意餐厅，我们提供配送队。"(01:44:15): 所以，他们打开了可用供给侧。现在，当我想 LLM，我觉得第三类有真机会。LLM 也许让带上一种供给侧成为可能——也许是长尾，那只是接触、入驻他们太费劲，但如果你自动化那工作，你其实创造了以我们现在谁都预料不到的方式扩展供给侧的机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very cool. Turned into AI corner, which I love. Okay, well, with that, we reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 很酷。变成 AI 角了，我爱。好，话虽如此，我们到了超刺激的闪电轮。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Okay, I'm ready.
turns.zh: 好，我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 你最常推荐给别人的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Pachinko is one of the best fictional books I've read in a while. I just loved it, and so, I highly recommend that. And then, to founders, I am a sucker for The Five Temptations of a CEO and The Five Dysfunctions of a Team. It's kind of like you imagine those books in the grocery store aisle, but they're fast reads that are incredibly insightful and I highly recommend.
turns.zh: 《柏青哥》（Pachinko）是我近期读最好的虚构书之一。我就是爱它，所以强烈推荐。然后，对创始人，我是《CEO 的五个诱惑》（The Five Temptations of a CEO）和《团队的五种功能障碍》（The Five Dysfunctions of a Team）的粉丝。就像你在杂货店过道想那些书，但它们读得快、洞察惊人，我强烈推荐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a favorite recent movie or TV show that you really enjoy?
turns.zh: 有最近很喜欢的一部电影或剧集吗？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: I don't watch stuff, so I'm not a good candidate there.
turns.zh: 我不看东西，所以我不是那的好人选。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I highly respect that. Is there a favorite interview question that you like to ask candidates, which usually, we can transform into when you're talking to founders and trying to decide if you want to invest?
turns.zh: 我高度尊重。你有喜欢问候选人的面试问题吗——通常我们能转成当你和创始人聊、决定要不要投？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: I always love hearing the journey people take and specifically how they've made decisions along the way, what drives them from each step. I think that's always very illuminating.
turns.zh: 我总爱听人们走的旅程、具体他们一路怎么做的决定、每步是什么驱使他们。我觉得那总很有启发。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really love, whether it's an app or physical product that you've used often? Anything real cool or fun?
turns.zh: 你有最近发现、真爱的产品吗，无论 App 还是你常用的实体产品？任何真酷或好玩的？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: I'll say we are late joiners to Tesla, my family. And man, it is one of those products that you use it for the first time, and you're just like, "I could see why I'd want to own equity in this company," not financial advice obviously, but it's just an awesome experience.
turns.zh: 我说我们家是 Tesla 的迟到加入者。而老兄，它是那种你第一次用、就"我能看为什么我想在这公司持点股"，显然不是财务建议，但它就是个超棒体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I completely agree. I've gotten so used to, we have a regular car and a Tesla, and the fact that you don't need a key anymore, you just walk up and open it, because it has your phone... My wife, she left the key in our Subaru, just because she's like, "Oh, shit, I need to take the key out." It's just sitting there running. Yeah, you're so used to just the casual just walk up, open, you're good to go. Awesome. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often repeat to yourself, share with people, either in work or life, that you find useful?
turns.zh: 我完全同意。我们太习惯——我们有辆普通车和的 Tesla，而事实是你不再需要钥匙，你走过去开它就开，因为它有你手机……我妻子，她把钥匙落在 Subaru 里，就因为"哦 shit，我得把钥匙拿出来。"它就停那运行着。对，你太习惯就随意走过去、开、走人。太棒了。你有常对自己重复、分享给人的座右铭吗，工作或生活里，你觉得有用？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: My partner at Greylock, Reid Hoffman, has this line of every strength has a corresponding weakness, and vice versa, and there's so much wisdom there. We see our own strengths and we see our weaknesses, but not realize that they actually go together. You can't have one without the other. Similarly, strengths in organizations, like a decentralized organization can move really quickly, and the corresponding weakness of that is that it can feel chaotic and disorganized. On the other side, a centralized organization can feel really slow, but it is very intentional in the decision-making and the control of the experience. And so, everything has trade-offs, and realizing that, more often than not, they come together, it's just so useful to be aware of that.
turns.zh: 我在 Greylock 的合伙人 Reid Hoffman 有句话：每个优势都有对应劣势，反之亦然（every strength has a corresponding weakness），那有太多智慧。我们看到自己优势、看到自己劣势，但没意识到它们其实连在一起。你不能有其一没其二。同理，组织的优势，像去中心化组织能移动很快，对应劣势是它感觉混乱无组织。另一边，中心化组织感觉很慢，但它在决策和体验控制上非常刻意。所以，一切有取舍，意识到那——大多时候它们一起来——意识到那太有用了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Final question. I believe you played rugby at some point, is that right?
turns.zh: 太棒了。最后一个问题。我相信你某时打过橄榄球，对吗？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Is there a rugby story that would be fun to share from your time playing rugby? And if not, what should people know? What would surprise people about rugby, that they may not be aware of?
turns.zh: 好。有打橄榄球时好玩分享的故事吗？如果没有，人们该知道什么？关于橄榄球什么会让人惊讶、他们也许不知道？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Well, what people might be surprised of, especially if they meet me, is that I was actually a really good tackler, and I think I broke my nose a couple times and have more injuries than I would care to remember, but I definitely inflicted more injuries on other people than I received. And I think rugby is, there's a camaraderie that comes with rugby, and the one thing I'll confess is that we always joke that the rugby team is, it's not a rugby team, it's a drinking team, that has a rugby problem.
turns.zh: 嗯，人们也许惊讶的，尤其如果他们见我，是我其实是个很好的擒抱手，我觉得我断过几次鼻、有比我想记的更多的伤，但我绝对施加给别人的伤比收到的多。我觉得橄榄球有种同志情谊，而我承认的一件事是我们总玩笑说橄榄球队不是橄榄球队，是个喝酒队、有个橄榄球问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing.
turns.zh: 惊人。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Those times are behind me.
turns.zh: 那些时光已在我身后。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man. It sounds like an awesome person to have in your court when you're a founder, the best tackler in town.
turns.zh: 哦老兄。听起来你是个创始人想要在身边的超棒的人，镇上最好的擒抱手。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Heck yes.
turns.zh: 绝对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Sarah, I'm not surprised this went as long as it did. Thank you so much for being here. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out and maybe ask follow-up questions? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 惊人。Sarah，我不惊讶这聊了这么久。非常感谢你来。两个最后问题。人们想联系、也许问后续问题，能在哪线上找到你？听众怎么对你有用？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: I appreciate that. I'm Sarah at Benchmark. I'm on Twitter, Sarah Tavel, and I have a Substack, SarahTavel.com. If you're a founder, you're working on something, don't be shy. We're in the business of meeting with people like you, and so, I always love to get stimulated by new ideas and people.
turns.zh: 我感激那个。我是 Benchmark 的 Sarah。我在 Twitter，Sarah Tavel，我有个 Substack，SarahTavel.com。如果你是创始人、在做某事，别害羞。我们就是做见你这样的人生意的，所以我总爱被新想法和人刺激。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to focus people even more there, is there stage you like, is there markets, anything people should know of what's right for you?
turns.zh: 就让人更聚焦那，有你喜欢的阶段吗，有市场吗，人们该知道的、什么适合你？

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: We, at Benchmark, we're early stage. We're an early stage firm. We aspire to be first board member. Usually, it looks like the series A, and that's really where our sweet spot is.
turns.zh: 我们，在 Benchmark，我们是早期。我们是早期基金。我们渴望成为第一个董事会成员。通常，看起来像 A 轮，那真是我们甜区。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Sarah, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。Sarah，非常感谢你来。

turns.speaker: Sarah Tavel
turns.en: Thank you for having me.
turns.zh: 谢谢邀请我。
